1.sense: The surah opens on an oath sworn by a feminine plural that is never named. Something pulls, and pulls to the very end, taking the whole of what it takes rather than part of it. The reader is given the action before he is given the actor.

notes.t: What the five oath groups of verses one to five refer to was never settled. Angels taking souls, the stars in their courses, the souls themselves, war horses, and the archer's bow have all been held by serious exegetes. At-Tabari lists the positions and does not choose one.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record several readings for each of the five

notes.t: Gharqan is a verbal noun from the root of drowning, used here as an adverb. It says the pulling goes to the furthest point, with nothing left behind in the place it came from.
The Qur'an does describe angels taking the souls of deniers harshly, striking their faces and their backs, which is the reading most exegetes bring to this verse.

links.why: another surah opening on an oath sworn by unnamed feminine plurals
a run of such oaths standing in front of a passage on the Hour

words.g: by those who draw out gently

2.sense: The second oath is the first one's opposite in manner. Where the first pulls hard, this one loosens and slips the thing free, the way a knot is undone rather than cut. Two ways of taking the same thing.

notes.t: Nashata is used in Arabic of untying a knot and of a bucket drawn up smoothly from a well. Set against the first oath it puts a hard taking beside an easy one.
Exegetes who read the first two oaths as angels of death read them as two kinds of dying, the denier's and the believer's. Others read both as stars moving from one station to the next.
notes.src: at-Tabari collects both readings without deciding

notes.t: The Qur'an does draw the contrast between the two receptions elsewhere: those whom the angels take in a good state are greeted with peace.

links.why: the gentle taking, and what is said to the one taken
the hard taking, with the angels' hands outstretched

3.sense: The third oath is on movement through a medium that offers no road. Swimming is how a body crosses water with no track laid for it, and the Qur'an uses the same verb of the sun and the moon in their courses.

notes.t: The same verb is used of the heavenly bodies: each one swimming in an orbit. That usage is why the reading of these oaths as stars has never gone away.
The three oaths so far move from a hard pull, to an easy release, to free travel. Whatever they name, the sequence loosens at every step.
Some early authorities read as-sabihat as ships, others as the souls of the believers travelling after death, others as the angels descending. The word itself decides nothing.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the several positions

links.why: each in an orbit, swimming
the same verb used of sun and moon keeping their courses

4.sense: The linking particle changes here from wa to fa, which in Arabic marks sequence rather than plain addition. The swimming becomes outstripping. These get there first.

notes.t: The shift from waw to fa at verses four and five is a grammatical signal, not a stylistic one. The first three items are listed side by side; the last two follow on from what came before them.
The Qur'an says of the angels that they do not get ahead of Him in speech and that they act by His command, which sets a limit on what any racing ahead can mean.
Readings of this fourth oath include the angels reaching the believing soul first, the stars overtaking one another, and horses at the charge. The exegetes who chose differed.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir list the positions

links.why: the limit placed on angelic initiative
there is not one of us without a known station

5.sense: The five oaths end on management. Something is carrying out an assignment, and the word for what it carries out is left indefinite, a matter, not the matter.

notes.t: The verb dabbara is used in the Qur'an of Allah Himself directing the affair from the heaven to the earth. Here the participle is applied to created things doing it under Him.
The participle is active, those who arrange, so whatever these are they are executing an order rather than issuing one. The Arabic keeps the agency borrowed.
This fifth oath is the one on which the exegetes come closest to agreement: most of the early authorities read it as the angels, while the first four stayed contested.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report the angels as the position of most of the early authorities here

links.why: He arranges the matter from the heaven to the earth
the same verb, with the command running through the created order

6.sense: The oaths are left without a stated answer. Instead the surah jumps to a Day and names it by the shaking that happens on it. Verb and noun come from one root, so the line says the shaker shakes, which in Arabic is emphasis and not repetition.

notes.t: The response to the oaths of verses one to five is never supplied in words. Arabic allows an omitted answer, and the exegetes fill it with something like: you will surely be raised. The gap leaves the five oaths pointing at this Day with no sentence to hold them down.
The Qur'an uses this same verb of the same Day elsewhere: on the Day the earth and the mountains convulse.
Whether ar-rajifah is the first blast of the Trumpet, the earth itself, or the general shaking of everything is read three ways. Most exegetes take it as the first blast.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the readings; the first blast is the commonest

links.why: the same verb naming the same Day
the two blowings of the Trumpet set out in full

7.sense: A second thing comes after the first, riding close behind it. Radif is the word for the person mounted behind the rider on the same animal, so the space between the two is not large.

notes.t: Abu Hurayra reported that between the two blasts is forty. He was asked forty days, forty months, forty years, and declined to specify each time. The number is given and its unit is not.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, the report of Abu Hurayra on what lies between the two blasts

notes.t: The Qur'an sets out what each blast does: at the first everyone in the heavens and the earth falls dead, at the second they are standing and looking on.
Verses six and seven give the whole architecture of the end in five Arabic words, then move straight to what it does to people. The event gets less space than the reaction to it.

links.why: the first blast and the second, described in order
the terror of everyone in the heavens and the earth at the blowing

8.sense: The view moves from the cosmos to the inside of a chest. Wajif is the knocking of a heart that has been frightened, the thing a person can feel in his own ribs. The word for hearts is indefinite, hearts and not the hearts, so it is some and not all.

notes.t: Hearts is left indefinite, which matters at the end of the surah. The verse does not say every heart, and verse forty describes people who did their fearing earlier and are not being described here.
The Qur'an describes the same state elsewhere as hearts arrived at the throats, with their owners choking on them.
Wajafa is used of the fast unsettled gait of a camel as well as of a heart. The word carries motion that will not come back to rest.

links.why: hearts at the throats on the Day of the Approaching
the convulsion of the Hour and what it does to people

9.sense: The eyes are given to the hearts rather than to people, which keeps the whole description inside the body. Khushu is the look of something that has stopped resisting: the eyes go down and stay down.

notes.t: The pronoun in absaruha refers back to hearts, so the Arabic reads literally as the eyes of the hearts. Grammarians explain it as the eyes of the people who own those hearts, and the compression keeps the fear internal rather than staged.
The same phrase, their eyes lowered, describes them elsewhere at the moment of coming out of the graves.
Khushu is also the word for the humility asked of a person in prayer. The same posture is chosen in one place and imposed in the other.

links.why: eyes lowered with humiliation covering them
the same look at the emergence from the graves

10.sense: The surah reaches back from the Day to what these people were saying while alive. The question is not asked for information. It is a way of refusing the answer before it arrives.

notes.t: Al-hafirah has three old readings. The Arabs said a man returned in his hafirah when he went back along his own hoof prints, so the first sense is the state he started from. Others read it as the grave, and others as the dug earth itself.
notes.src: at-Tabari collects all three senses

notes.t: The passive form matters. They do not ask whether they are going back, they ask whether they are to be sent back, which concedes in the grammar that somebody else would be doing it.
The Qur'an records the same objection in their mouths in other words: when we are lost within the earth, will we be in a new creation.

links.why: the objection stated in its standard form, bones and crumbled dust
that is a return from far off

11.sense: They name the state they expect to be in, and they pick the least promising material they can think of. Nakhirah is bone gone hollow, the kind that sounds when air passes through it.

notes.t: Two canonical readings stand at this word, the short nakhirah and the longer nakhirah with an alif after the first letter. Hafs, the reading of this Mushaf, has the shorter form. The sense is close either way.
notes.src: the canonical readings differ at this word; Hafs reads nakhirah

notes.t: The root n-kh-r is used of a decayed tree trunk that whistles when the wind moves inside it. Their argument is a material one, taken from what they have watched happen to a body.
The Qur'an answers this exact objection elsewhere by naming who made the bone in the first place, and calls the objector someone who forgot his own creation.

links.why: who will give life to bones when they have crumbled
the same argument put in almost the same words

12.sense: They finish the argument with a joke. If it happens at all, they say, it will go badly for us. The line is sarcasm, and the surah records it without softening it.

notes.t: Khasirah is the merchant's word for a deal that came back short. They concede, for the sake of the argument, that a return would put them on the wrong side of the accounting, and they treat that as a reason not to believe in it.
The same word karrah comes back later in the Qur'an in the mouths of the same kind of people, no longer as a joke: if only we had a return, so that we could be among the believers.

The verb moves from the present in verse ten to the past here. One reading takes both as reports of what they habitually said; another reads the second as what they will say when they see it and finds the past tense used for a thing already certain.
notes.src: at-Tabari notes the shift of tense and the readings of it

links.why: the same word asked for in earnest once it is too late
if only I had one more turn, so that I could be among the doers of good

13.sense: The reply to the whole objection is one clause long. Whatever they imagine the difficulty to be, the cost of it is one shout. No process is described because none is needed.

notes.t: Zajrah is not noise in general. It is the shout a herdsman uses to drive an animal, a sound given as a command. What brings the dead back is an order rather than a mechanism.
The identical phrase, it is only one shout, appears in as-Saffat with the same result following straight after it.
Fa-innama is the strongest restriction the language has. It shuts out every other possibility rather than naming the likeliest one.

links.why: the same sentence, followed by the same sudden standing
one shout, and at once they are all present before Us

14.sense: There is no verb of rising or coming out. One moment the shout, the next moment they are simply there, on a flat exposed surface with nothing on it.

notes.t: As-sahirah is read by most exegetes as the surface of the earth, a bare open plain. It comes from the root of staying awake, and one explanation is that the plain is called sleepless because nothing sleeps on it. Others read it as the name of a particular place.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the surface of the earth and several named places

notes.t: The Qur'an describes the ground of that Day as levelled off, with no dip and no rise left anywhere in it.
The idha of surprise is what makes the line land. Arabic has a particle for something arriving without an interval, and there is no interval here between the shout and the standing.

links.why: the earth left as a level plain with nothing standing on it
the Day the earth is exchanged for another earth

15.sense: The subject changes without a bridge. A question is put to the Prophet ﷺ, and the surah leaves the Day in order to tell a story about a man who was warned in person and refused.

notes.t: The question is not asking whether he knows. It is a way of handing a story over, and it makes the listener sit up before the first line of it arrives.
The Qur'an opens the same episode with the same question in Ta-Ha, and uses the formula elsewhere for the guests of Ibrahim and for the armies of Pharaoh and Thamud.

Musa is named more times in the Qur'an than any other prophet, and his confrontation with Pharaoh is retold more often than any other single episode. Here it is given ten verses and no dialogue from Musa after verse nineteen.

links.why: the same question opening the same story at greater length
the same formula used of Pharaoh and Thamud together

16.sense: The whole of the calling is compressed into one line: a voice, a place, and a name for the place. Musa was not sent a message through anyone. He was called directly, in a valley he had walked into looking for fire.

notes.t: Tuwa is read two ways. Some take it as the proper name of the valley. Others take it as a word meaning folded or done twice, so that the valley was sanctified twice over or that Musa was called there twice.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both the proper name and the sense of folded or twice-done

notes.t: The fuller account of the same night is in Ta-Ha, where he is told to take off his sandals because he is in the sanctified valley of Tuwa.
The canonical readers differ over whether Tuwa carries tanwin. Hafs, the reading of this Mushaf, gives it tanwin; others read it without. Nothing in the meaning turns on it.
notes.src: a difference among the canonical readings, not between sound and weak

links.why: the same call given at length, with what was said in it
the call named as coming from the right side of the valley, from the tree

17.sense: The instruction is short and it comes with a reason attached. Tagha is the verb for water that has broken past its banks, and the charge against Pharaoh through the whole surah is that he went past a limit, not that he held a wrong opinion.

notes.t: The same command in the same four words is given in Ta-Ha, which is the closest verbal parallel to this passage anywhere in the Qur'an.

The Qur'an uses tagha of the flood water that rose past what should have held it, which fixes the image behind the word: not wickedness in the abstract, but a thing that will not stay inside its edge.
The same verb comes back at verse thirty-seven with no name attached to it, which puts Pharaoh's crime in a category open to anyone listening.

links.why: the identical command given at the same moment of the story
the same errand described as going to a wrongdoing people

18.sense: The message to the tyrant opens as an offer and not as a threat. The Arabic idiom is close to would you care to, and it leaves the man free to say no without being cornered.

notes.t: Hal laka ila such and such is an offer phrased so that the other person can decline without losing face. It is what Musa is told to put to a man who would shortly claim to be a god.
In Ta-Ha the two brothers are told to speak to him a gentle word, in the hope that he might take heed or fear, which is the same instruction given as a manner rather than a sentence.
Tazakka is the verb behind the Qur'an's shortest definition of success: he has succeeded who purified himself. The offer made to Pharaoh is the same offer made to everyone.

links.why: the tone the errand was to be carried out in
the same verb naming what a person is for

19.sense: The offer has a second half, and it ends on an outcome most people would not present as an attraction. Musa is offering the man fear, and offering it as the good part.

notes.t: Your Lord, said to a man who is about to tell a crowd that he is theirs. The possessive settles the argument without arguing it.
The Qur'an makes the same link in the other direction: it is those of His servants who have knowledge who fear Allah. Fear follows from knowing rather than replacing it.
Khashya in the Qur'an is not panic. It is the wariness of somebody who has worked out who he is dealing with, which is why guidance is named here as the thing that produces it.

links.why: the ones who fear Him are the ones who know Him
the reward named for whoever feared his Lord

20.sense: The offer ends and the evidence is produced. The verse does not say which sign, only that it was the largest one available, and that it was shown to Pharaoh in person.

notes.t: Which sign this was is read several ways. Most exegetes take it as the staff turning into a serpent, some as the hand drawn out white, some as the two of them together.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report the staff, the hand, and both

notes.t: Musa is told in Ta-Ha, before he goes, that he is being shown some of the greatest signs of his Lord, using the same adjective that stands here.
The verb is showed, not argued. What follows in the next verse is a refusal that comes after the evidence rather than instead of it.

links.why: the greatest signs promised before the errand begins
the staff thrown down in front of Pharaoh

21.sense: Two words for the whole response. He called it a lie, which is what he said, and he disobeyed, which is what he did. The Qur'an separates them because a man can do either one without the other.

notes.t: Kadhdhaba is not being mistaken about something. It is the intensive form, to declare a thing false, and declaring a thing false requires having heard it first.
Ta-Ha gives the same pair after all the signs had been shown: We showed him Our signs, all of them, and he denied and refused.
Nothing stands between verse twenty and verse twenty-one. The sign and the denial are joined by fa, the particle of immediate result, so there is no interval in which he weighed it.

links.why: the same refusal after the full set of signs
they rejected the signs while their own selves were convinced by them

22.sense: He does not merely walk away. He turns round and goes at speed, which means the walking away was itself work he had to put effort into.

notes.t: Yas'a is a circumstantial clause: he turned his back in a state of striving. The energy that could have gone into the offer goes into getting clear of it.
Ta-Ha describes the same movement and names what he was hurrying to do, which was to assemble his plan and then come back with it.
Thumma marks a gap in time, unlike the fa of the verse before. The denial was immediate; the organising took a while, and the surah lets you feel the difference.

links.why: what the hurrying was for
the summoning of the magicians from every city

23.sense: Two verbs, both of them public. He assembles people and then addresses them, which is how the claim in the next verse gets made: not privately to himself but as an announcement to a crowd.

notes.t: Hashara is the verb the Qur'an uses for the gathering on the Day of Resurrection. Pharaoh holds his own assembly and makes his own proclamation at it, and the surah has already shown, twenty verses earlier, what the real one looks like.
Nada is the same verb used at verse sixteen for the call that reached Musa. One call came from the Lord of the valley, the other from a man on a platform, and the surah uses one word for both.
The Qur'an records him elsewhere calling out among his people and asking whether the kingdom of Egypt is not his, and whether these rivers do not run beneath him.

links.why: the speech he made to the assembled people
the crowd called together to watch

24.sense: The claim is made with an adjective, and the adjective ranks rather than excludes. He is not denying that other lords exist. He is putting himself at the top of a list.

notes.t: The highest is a ranking word. It concedes a hierarchy and claims the top of it, which is a smaller and much commoner claim than outright denial, and an easier one for a crowd to accept.
Elsewhere he puts the same thing as ignorance rather than assertion: I have not known you to have any god other than me. The two forms are the polite and the blunt version of one position.
Al-A'la is a name of Allah, and it stands at the head of another surah in the command to glorify it. Pharaoh takes the word and fastens it to himself.

links.why: the same claim in its milder wording
the name he borrowed, in its place

25.sense: The name Allah appears here for the first time since the story began. Between the claim in verse twenty-four and the seizing there is one particle. The verse gives no account of the drowning, only that the matter was dealt with.

notes.t: The last and the first is read two ways. One reading has it as the punishment of the Hereafter and of this world. The other has it as his two sayings, the last being I am your lord most high and the first being I have not known you to have any god other than me.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both readings and neither is weak

notes.t: Nakal is not simply punishment. It is a penalty made public so that others are held back by the sight of it, which is why the Qur'an says elsewhere that his body was preserved as a sign for those who came after.

Al-Muzzammil gives the same sequence and states plainly who the warning is for: We sent to you a messenger as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh, and Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger, so We seized him with a ruinous seizure.

links.why: the same seizing turned into a warning to the Prophet ﷺ's own audience
the body preserved so that later people would have a sign

26.sense: The story closes by naming who it works on. Not whoever hears it and not whoever is clever, but whoever fears. That is the same verb Musa offered to Pharaoh at verse nineteen, and Pharaoh did not take it.

notes.t: Ibrah comes from a root meaning to cross over, the same root as the word for interpreting a dream. A lesson in Arabic is something you pass through from one side to the other, from the case in front of you to your own case.
The Qur'an uses the same word of the prophetic stories generally: in their accounts there is a lesson for people who have minds.
The root kh-sh-y runs through the surah at three points, verse nineteen, this verse, and verse forty-five. It is the surah's own test for whether anything said in it will land on a listener.

links.why: the stories described as a lesson for those with minds
the direct command to take the lesson, addressed to people with eyes

27.sense: The argument turns back on the objection of verse eleven. If the problem is that raising a crumbled body would be too hard, then set the body beside the sky and say which of the two is the harder build.

notes.t: The Qur'an states the comparison flatly elsewhere: the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most of the people do not know it.
He built it arrives as a separate short sentence directly after the question, before the questioner can answer. The Arabic switches from asking to describing and never returns to the question.
The sky is chosen because it was the largest thing anyone in that audience had ever looked at, and because none of them had built anything remotely like it.

links.why: the comparison stated instead of asked
is the One who made the heavens and the earth not able to make their like

28.sense: Two operations on the same object, in the order a builder would do them. First the height, then the finish. Samk is the measure of a thing from bottom to top, the word for how tall a wall has been taken.

notes.t: The building vocabulary is kept consistent across three verses: built it, raised its height, evened it out. The Qur'an is describing the sky in the words a person would use about a house.
The Qur'an says of the same sky that you will find no flaw in it, and it invites the eye to go back over it twice and come back tired.
Sawwa means to bring a thing to proportion, with no part that does not fit the rest. The same verb is used of the making of a human being, which is the other half of the comparison.

links.why: the invitation to look for a crack in it
the sky built with strength, and the builder still expanding it

29.sense: The night and the morning are both attached to the sky by a possessive, its night and its morning, as if they were features of the building rather than things that happen to us. One is darkened and the other is brought out, and both are done to it.

notes.t: Aghtasha is a rare verb and this is its only use in the Qur'an. Putting the darkness in the active voice makes it something done rather than something that merely occurs when the light leaves.
The Qur'an pairs the two the same way in the short oaths: by the night when it covers over, and the day when it shows itself.
Duha is not dawn. It is the light of mid-morning, when the sun is well up, and the word is used to name the whole daytime by its clearest hour. It returns as the last word of the surah.

links.why: the same pair sworn by in the same order
sun, moon, day and night set out as a sequence of signs

30.sense: An order is stated: the sky first, then the earth spread. The verse does not say the earth was created after the sky. It says it was spread out after, which is a different operation on a thing that was already there.

notes.t: This verse and the passage in Fussilat, which puts the earth's making before the heaven's, were put to Ibn Abbas as a contradiction. The answer reported from him is that the earth was created first and its spreading, the dahw, came afterwards. The reconciliation is his and other exegetes offered others.
notes.src: at-Tabari collects the reports from Ibn ʿAbbās on this pairing

notes.t: The root d-h-w means to spread out and level, and the same root gives the word for the shallow hollow an ostrich scrapes to lay in. Modern claims that the verb means to make egg-shaped read the egg back into a word the lexicographers used for the ground underneath it.
The same act is described with a different verb in al-Hijr, where the earth is spread out and firm mountains are cast into it.

links.why: the passage that gives the making in the other order
what is on the earth made first, then attention turned to the heaven

31.sense: Two things come out of the spread ground, and they are named in the order a herdsman would name them. Water first, then what grows because of the water.

notes.t: Mar'a is grazing land specifically, not vegetation in general. The vocabulary belongs to people who kept animals, and the audience of this surah did.
Abasa sets out the same sequence at length, with the water poured and the ground split open, and ends the list on the same two beneficiaries this surah names two verses later.
From it, minha, is doing work in the line. The water is not described as arriving from somewhere else; the earth itself is made to yield it.

links.why: the same argument spelled out crop by crop
water sent down, and the pasture that comes up because of it

32.sense: The mountains get one verb and it is a mooring word. Arsa is what is done to a ship to stop it drifting, and the same root gives the word for an anchorage.

notes.t: The Qur'an gives the reason elsewhere: He cast firm mountains into the earth so that it would not sway with you.
The same root, r-s-w, comes back at verse forty-two in the question about when the Hour drops anchor. One image serves for a mountain set in the ground and for a day set in time.
An-Naba puts the same idea in a noun and calls the mountains pegs, using the word for a tent stake.

links.why: the mountains given a stated purpose
the same fact in the image of a tent peg

33.sense: The whole build is summed up in one purpose clause, and the purpose is a modest one. The sky, the night, the water and the mountains are called supplies, and the list of who they are for includes the animals.

notes.t: The identical phrase, word for word, closes the same argument in Abasa. Two surahs run the same case and arrive at the same three words.

Mata is temporary provision, the goods a person takes on a trip and leaves behind at the end of it. The word has an expiry inside it, which is why the next verse can arrive without changing the subject.
The address turns to you here for the first time since verse twenty-seven. The evidence was laid out in the third person and the bill is handed over in the second.

links.why: the same three words closing the same argument
the livestock described from the user's side, warmth and carriage and food

34.sense: The provision ends and the ending gets a name. Tammah is a calamity that goes over the top of everything, the way water rises past a wall, and it is qualified as the greatest, which implies there have been smaller ones.

notes.t: The root t-m-m is used of a flood topping what should have contained it, which is the same picture as the tagha of verse seventeen. Every earlier disaster in the surah, the drowning of Pharaoh included, is a smaller version of this one.
Abasa opens the matching passage with the same construction and a different name for the same event, as-Sakhkhah, the deafening blow.
Al-kubra was last used at verse twenty for the sign shown to Pharaoh. The greatest sign was refused. The greatest event will not be.

links.why: the same sentence shape with the Day under another name
a whole surah built on one more name for it

35.sense: The Day is defined by an act of memory. At this point in the verse nothing new is shown to him. He is simply made to recall what he spent himself on.

notes.t: Sa'a is the verb used of Pharaoh at verse twenty-two, where he turned his back hurrying. What a person hurried after is the thing set in front of him here.
Al-Fajr gives the same line and adds the difficulty with it: man will remember on that Day, and what will the remembering do for him then.
Elsewhere the Qur'an says he will be informed of what he sent ahead and what he left behind, so the memory is not left to his own honesty.

links.why: the same remembering, with its uselessness stated
informed of what he sent forward and what he held back

36.sense: The second thing shown is not a report of the Fire but the Fire itself, moved out into the open. The qualifier is the odd part: for whoever sees, rather than for whoever is guilty.

notes.t: Burrizat is an intensive passive, made to appear, brought out from where it had been. The verse says nothing about the Fire being made at that moment, only about it becoming visible.
The same verb with the same object appears in ash-Shu'ara with a narrower qualifier, brought out for those who had gone astray.
For whoever sees leaves the seeing open rather than restricting it. Everyone present has eyes, so the phrase reads less as a limit than as a statement that there will be nothing else in view.

links.why: the same verb and object with a different qualifier
the Fire brought forward on the same Day as the remembering

37.sense: The verb used of Pharaoh at verse seventeen is now used with no name attached to it. The category he was in is open, and the surah has just spent ten verses showing what it looks like from the inside.

notes.t: Fa-amma opens the first of a matched pair of clauses. Arabic uses the amma construction to sort a group into two, and the surah spends five verses doing exactly that.
The Qur'an uses the same verb of people in general and gives its trigger: man oversteps when he sees himself as needing no one.
No crime is named here beyond the overstepping itself and the preference in the next verse. Between them the two cover a whole life without requiring one spectacular sin.

links.why: the same verb with self-sufficiency named as its cause
the peoples who overstepped in the lands, listed by name

38.sense: The second half of the charge is a preference and not a denial. He did not have to say there was no other life. He chose this one while both were in front of him.

notes.t: Athara means to prefer one thing over another when both are available, which requires knowing about the second. The word assumes the man had heard the message and weighed it.
Al-A'la states the same charge and answers it in the next line: rather you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and longer lasting.
Ad-dunya is a comparative, the nearer one. Arabic names this life by its closeness rather than by anything inside it, which already frames the choice as proximity over value.

links.why: the same preference named and then priced
those who love this life more, and what follows from it

39.sense: The word for the destination is ma'wa, the place a person comes back to at the end of a day and shelters in. The Fire is described in the vocabulary of home.

notes.t: Ma'wa is where a traveller ends up and stops. Using it here says the man arrived somewhere rather than that something was done to him, which matches a verse whose only charges were a preference and an overstepping.
The definite article, the refuge rather than his refuge, makes it the refuge as such, the only shelter on offer to him.
The Qur'an uses the same noun of the Garden, calling it jannat al-ma'wa, so both ends of this pair share one word.

links.why: the same noun used of the other destination
the Fire named as the refuge of those who set up partners

40.sense: The other column. Two conditions, and both of them happen where nobody can check: a fear nobody sees, and a refusal only the one refusing ever hears.

notes.t: Maqam rabbihi is read two ways. One reading is the place where he will stand in front of his Lord. The other is his Lord's standing over him, taken from the verse about the One who stands over every soul with what it has earned. Both are old.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both, with the second leaning on 13:33

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ named seven whom Allah will shade on a Day with no shade but His. Two of them belong in this verse: the man who refused a woman of beauty and standing saying that he feared Allah, and the man who remembered Allah alone until his eyes overflowed.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, the report of the seven whom Allah shades

notes.t: Hawa is what the self leans toward, from a root meaning to fall. The verse does not ask for the craving to be absent. It asks for the self to be told no, which assumes the craving is there.

links.why: two gardens promised in nearly these words to whoever feared the standing
the self described as pushing hard toward what it wants

41.sense: The sentence mirrors verse thirty-nine with one word changed. The matching says that the two outcomes are the same kind of thing reached by two different routes.

notes.t: Four words in each half of the pair, and the only difference between them is the noun. The Qur'an lets the symmetry carry the point that nothing separates the two cases except what the person did.
The Prophet ﷺ said that the Garden is fenced about with the things the self dislikes and the Fire is fenced about with its cravings, which is the same division this pair of verses makes.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, the report that Paradise is screened by hardships and the Fire by desires

notes.t: The Garden is described here by shelter alone and by none of its contents, which is what keeps it matched to verse thirty-nine rather than outweighing it.

links.why: the Garden of Refuge named with the same word
the same Garden placed at the furthest point of the ascent

42.sense: The surah turns back to the questioners. They want a date, and the word they use for its arrival is a sailor's word: when does it drop anchor.

notes.t: Mursa is from the same root as arsaha at verse thirty-two, where the mountains were moored. The Hour is spoken of as a ship already at sea, waiting only to be tied up.
Al-A'raf records the identical question in the identical words and answers it at length, which makes this the shorter of two treatments of one exchange.
When Jibril came in the form of a man and asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Hour, the answer given was that the one being asked knows no more about it than the one asking.
notes.src: the hadith of Jibril, Bukhari 50 and Muslim 8

links.why: the same question with the full answer attached
people asking about the Hour and being told where its knowledge sits

43.sense: The reply is a question put back, and it takes the Prophet ﷺ out of the business of dating the Hour entirely. He is not the one holding that information.

notes.t: The sense of the line is read two ways. One reading makes it a rebuke of the askers: what have you to do with mentioning it. The other makes it a statement about the Prophet ﷺ, that his being sent is itself one of the signs of its nearness, so his position is its mention.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both readings of the line

notes.t: The question form is what does the refusing. Answering a request for a date with a question about the asker's standing declines it more firmly than a plain no would.
The Qur'an elsewhere has him say outright that he holds no benefit or harm for himself except as Allah wills, and that he is only a warner and a bringer of good news.

links.why: the same limit stated as a first person declaration
the Hour listed among the things no one else holds

44.sense: Where it stops is named. The Arabic puts to your Lord in front of the subject, which is how the language says only there and nowhere else.

notes.t: The fronting of ila rabbika is the same device as You alone we worship in al-Fatiha. Putting the destination before the thing that reaches it is how Arabic restricts without a word for only.
An-Najm makes the same statement about everything and not only about the Hour: to your Lord is the finality.
Muntaha is the point past which a thing does not go. The verse does not say Allah knows when the Hour is, it says the Hour terminates with Him, which covers the knowing and the deciding in one word.

links.why: the same construction applied to every end and not just this one
the knowledge of the Hour referred back to Him alone

45.sense: The job is described with a restriction at both ends. He is only a warner, and the warning is described as landing on people who already have some fear in them.

notes.t: The root kh-sh-y has now been used three times in this surah: offered to Pharaoh at verse nineteen, made the condition of the lesson at verse twenty-six, and made the audience of the warning here. It is the surah's own test for whether any of it will take.
Fatir says the same and fills in who those people are: you only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and establish the prayer.
Qaf gives the identical instruction as a command: so remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning.

links.why: the same limit with the audience described
the same job given as an order rather than a description

words.g: it will be as though they

46.sense: The surah ends with a life measured from the far side of it. Not years, and not even a day: an evening, or the morning that follows one. The whole span they were arguing about the return of turns out to fit between sunset and mid-morning.

notes.t: Duha closes the surah and it was used at verse twenty-nine of the morning light brought out over the world. The word that named the daylight now measures a human lifetime, and it is the last word in the surah.
The Qur'an gives the same reckoning in other places, where they answer that they stayed a day or part of a day, and in al-Ahqaf as an hour of a day.
An evening or its morning is how a person describes a nap. The verse does not claim the life was short in fact. It says that is how long it will look to them at the moment they see the Hour.

links.why: the same sentence built on an hour of a day
the argument among them over whether it was ten days or one
